"executive_summary": "This study investigates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles (silver, gold, copper oxide, zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, and silicon dioxide) and three soluble salts (CuSO4, ZnSO4, and AgNO3) on the hatching of Artemia sp. cysts and the viability of early nauplii. The researchers used Artemia as a model organism due to its robustness, cost-effectiveness, and global distribution in highly saline waters. The physicochemical properties of the nanoparticles were characterized using TEM and DLS, and their behavior in both normal and marine water was analyzed. Hydrated and bleached Artemia cysts were allowed to hatch in aerated, filtered sterile salt water containing nanoparticles, and hatching rates were recorded. In parallel, a standard Artemia toxicity test was conducted on the nauplii to monitor viability. The toxicity of the nanoparticles was compared, and the order of toxicity was estimated as Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2. The study found a strong inverse correlation between hatching rates and larval mortality, suggesting that hatching rate can be used as a bioassay for hazard assessment of nanoparticles. The results also showed that silver and copper oxide nanoparticles had the highest toxicity, while silicon nanoparticles at low concentrations were conducive to hatching. The study highlights the potential of Artemia as a model organism for assessing nanoparticle ecotoxicity and suggests that these acute toxicity tests can be used as pre-screening tests for nanoparticle toxicity prior to validating them for in vivo toxicity studies. The study also notes that the toxicity of the nanoparticles could be due to their ionic forms, and that the nanoparticles remained stable in seawater up to one week, though the ionic or dissolved component may settle down due to precipitation. The study does not report the sample sizes, the specific concentrations used, or the statistical methods used to analyze the data, which limits the reproducibility of the study. The study also does not report the ethical considerations of using Artemia as a model organism, and the potential risks to the environment and human health from the release of these nanoparticles. Overall, the study provides valuable insights into the toxicity of engineered nanoparticles on Artemia sp., and highlights the potential of Artemia as a model organism for assessing nanoparticle ecotoxicity.",
